doc.title: Percy Heath — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
title: Never the same solo twice, unlike solos that became arrangements
summary: Heath contrasts the MJQ's fresh improvisation with fixed solos like 'Flying Home' and 'Cotton Tail'.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Let me tell you, John Lewis set up… he knew, if he did a certain thing, what Jackson would do. They were unbelievable. I played with those people for forty years and I never heard them play the same thing twice. They may have the same vocabulary, but never the same thing in the same place in thousands of concerts. Thousands. They never repeated. Like the solo of “Flying Home,” if you didn’t play that solo of Illinois Jacquet, you didn’t play the tune. I don’t care what tenor player it was. If you didn’t play that Illinois Jacquet solo, you didn’t play “Flying Home.” But there was never a repeat after the theme, which even that changed occasionally, they would embellish that somehow, but they never played the same. Improvise was improvise for the Modern Jazz Quartet, not [a] rehearsed solo, like Lester Young’s “D.V. Blues” and all that, and Count Basie, some of those solos, they played the same, like Ben Webster’s “Cotton Tail,” he played that, which became “Cotton Tail,” the song.
Where the solo becomes like an arrangement.
Where the solo became the song actually. But that never happened with the Modern Jazz Quartet. After the theme, it was never the same.
